story_text.value:
I recently bought 1993 TDM 850 and I love it, but its an old bike and it needed some TLC, I bought the haynes manual and the found the partlist and used Astra to create an interactive atlas.

I am working on the front forks now to change the bushings and seals, and I dont think I would've been able to do it without the interactive visualization, the partlist was not detailed enough and the manual was too prescriptive.

It gaslit me few times, so I had to use some common sense (like this spring can not be pushing this piece, stop trying to convince me it does), but over all it was a major help.

If you have an old machine, car, tractor, commodore64 etc, that is well documented, using Astra you can make amazing interface to see into it. It feels like early stages of the tooling Tony Stark had while creating Badassium :)

I cant wait for AR and models baked into hardware at 10 watts and 15000 tokens per second.

story_text.value:
I am a digital design engineer, and my day job is designing chips (mostly IP blocks, not full chips) in SystemVerilog. At the start of 2026 I started experimenting with LLM agents like Claude and Codex, and realized that they are very capable not just at software and scripts, but at hardware design as well! But after the initial excitement, I started running into repeating failures and friction:

- In chip design, we run a lot of heavy EDA tools: simulation, synthesis, linters. LLM agents often skipped those checks unless explicitly prompted - SystemVerilog code is not executed line-by-line as program code is. The different blocks of code are executed simultaneously, which makes it very hard to reason about the code in your head. Engineers typically simulate the code and analyze the waveforms, but agents can’t do it effectively (they are not great with visual information) - They selected the wrong configuration or misunderstood tool reports - Their generated tests concentrated on happy paths. - Giving them enough permissions to work independently put the dev machine at risk

But, despite the shortcomings, the potential was there! So I started fixing the failure modes one at a time, creating scripts, skills, isolating dev in docker… Over time, this work grew into one coherent system. I spent significant effort on user experience, documentation and debugging, and now I am happy to show it to the world

Booley combines open-source chip-design EDA tools and agent CLIs in one sandbox, using VScode as GUI. The tight integration between agents and EDA tools (via MCP) allows agents to use EDA effectively, plus you don’t have to maintain your own scripts and solve “works on my machine” issues. Booley gives the agent a way to inspect waveforms using CLI (custom Rust binary that parses simulation traces) and allows humans to define strict deterministically-enforced criteria to shape agentic work (”area must be reduced by 10% or more”, “this test must pass and catch 9/10 mutations of the device under test”).

I am not a professional software engineer myself (using LLMs helps, but not a silver bullet ofc), so any feedback from actual software devs is especially appreciated.

Github page includes demonstration videos and quick start demo

title.value: Show HN: Booley – open-source IDE for agentic chip design

Hi, I am building a FOSS life-management app.

Desktop & mobile.

Bills, recipes, inventory, goals, ideas, general notes, reminders with alarm sounds...

You can use AI to push/get data on it (completely optional, nothing built-in into it). You can disable features. You can self-host and run your own instance, same app with the same capabilities.

I've been developing it for 6 months already, for my personal usage, and have recently released it under a FOSS license.

The code is available at https://github.com/ontoplano/ontoplano

Any feedback is appreciated!

story_text.value:
Solo dev. built in my spare time.

Raven uses a combination of steganography and cryptography to create a metadata resistant messenger. It encrypts any piece of text on your device and stores the ciphertext on Solana. It works pairwise with keys, users decrypt locally on their device- no accounts. I do run the relayer and a retention sweeper (not claiming peer to peer). One more thing, every write is signed by the same pool wallet, so anyone can see volume/timing. Check the white paper below and there’s been no audit.

Several variations include: public, private, and stealth (for fun, i’ve hidden a public raven in this post)

White Paper: https://oara.ai/raven-whitepaper

The crypto and encoding core is open source. Apps are not open yet. Open source: https://github.com/OAraLabs/raven-core

iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/raven-hidden-messages/id677947...

Chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/raven-%E2%80%94-hid...

For fun public raven read key: https://sendraven.ink/k/Ot2YzGEoYYaMN1Uc

title.value: Show HN: Raven – Encrypted messages hidden inside ordinary text

story_text.value:
I built LazyReader because I was tired of re-importing the same ebook library whenever I switched devices or reading apps.

Most reading apps copy your books into their own storage. LazyReader connects directly to your existing cloud storage, so your books stay where they already are.

It supports Dropbox, OneDrive, and Nextcloud. You can browse your library and read EPUBs directly from the cloud, and it now also supports streaming audiobooks directly from cloud storage. So if you have a 1GB M4B audiobook, you don't need to download the entire file to your phone before listening.

Since the original version, LazyReader has grown into a much more complete reading app:

- EPUB and audiobook support - Library and reading-progress synchronization - Collections and sorting - EPUB and audiobook edition linking - Offline reading and listening - Offline dictionary - Word and phrase search - Notes and highlighting - Text-to-speech - Theming - Multiple cover-enrichment options - Book metadata editing - QR-code book sharing - Interactive/choice-driven EPUB support

The interactive EPUB support is probably one of the more unusual parts. EPUBs can contain much more structure than a typical linear ebook, so LazyReader can handle branching and choice-driven books as well as conventional EPUBs.

The main idea is still the same as when I started it: your books are your files, and your cloud storage is your storage. LazyReader doesn't require you to import everything into another proprietary library.

"LazyReader on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.lindocode....

Requires an account so your library, reading progress, and cloud-storage connections can be synchronized across devices.

I'd be interested in hearing what people think, especially about the cloud-based approach and audiobook streaming. Happy to answer questions about the implementation or anything else.
